9046: The management of sharks and rays in European fisheries is both complex and challenging. Compounding factors are paucity of data, the group TAC for skates and rays and the uncertainties surrounding the landing obligation, whereby the species could choke the target fisheries. Cooperation between multiple stakeholders is essential to address these issues. In order to do this, the Dutch Elasmobranch Society has organized a number of expert meetings in Amsterdam. The meetings were attended by scientists, administrators and representatives from the fishing industry and NGOs from six European countries. Possible solutions and ways forward were discussed and the delegates gave their support for the continuation of the platform and working towards solutions. In the coming years the partners in this project will work on developing a two track approach to addressing key issues and questions. On the one hand we will work on a science-industry partnership on solutions to collect essential information on bycatch and survival of elasmobranchs. On the other hand we will set up a dialogue platform with all stakeholders, in which ideas can be developed, coalitions formed and concrete solutions found. The resulting proposals to policy makers will have a high chance of successful implementation because they are supported by all relevant stakeholders. This unique approach combines multiple levels of influence. This presentation will present the first results of the multi-stakeholder process and co-production of knowledge for the management of elasmobranchs.
9047: Without understanding what factors inform shark movement decisions, assessments of interactions with area-focused human activities, such as fishing, and efforts to mitigate these interactions may be severely hindered. In the northwest Atlantic, Tiger Sharks are regularly caught in high seas fisheries, and have been shown to undertake long distance, partial migrations between coral reef and open ocean habitats. We used generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) to reveal how variation in intrinsic (e.g. size) and extrinsic factors (e.g. habitat suitability, prey availability) influenced migratory behaviour, and assessed how these migrations influence fisheries interactions and potential management strategies. We revealed that large Tiger Sharks primarily associated with a narrow thermal niche and areas of high primary productivity, while smaller sharks experienced a much broader range of temperatures and much weaker associations with productivity, indicating an ontogenetic shift in drivers of movements and migrations. The observed migration patterns have significant management implications: existing shark sanctuaries (Bahamas, British Virgin Islands, Saba) only covered 12% of Tiger Shark movements, although this could be increased to 52% through designation of Bermuda's exclusive economic zone as a shark sanctuary. However, evaluation of potential fisheries interactions revealed that over 80% of potential interactions would still occur outside of shark sanctuaries, requiring combination with other management interventions such as gear modification or quotas.
9048: Natural mortality is a crucial parameter to assess the status of species. However, it is inherently difficult to observe directly in nature and most commonly indirect methods are utilized to estimate natural mortality based on other life history parameters. These relationships are almost exclusively based on bony fish data and their performance for elasmobranchs is unclear due to a lack of data for this group. Here, we will present 15 direct estimates of natural mortality from 10 different elasmobranch species obtained from newly analysed datasets and an extensive literature review which is to our knowledge the world's most comprehensive dataset of its kind. We will discuss the performance of the most commonly applied indirect methods and give recommendations on best practices to estimate the natural mortality rate in elasmobranchs and other animals.
9049: The Dutch Caribbean islands are home to over 24 elasmobranch species, half of which are considered threatened with extinction according to IUCN guidelines. Over the past decades, local populations appear to have declined drastically, most probably due to fishing and loss of suitable habitat. There is a persistent lack of (baseline) data on their occurrence, spatial distribution, and population structure, which is an incentive for extensive biological research to scope the problem and underpin management advice. The utility of Ecological Risk Assessments is considered an effective tool to theoretically assess the vulnerability to fishing and habitat degradation of species for which there is little information available. For elasmobranch species, a semi-quantitative approach such as Productivity Susceptibility Analysis (PSA) may provide some insight into conservation and management priorities by assessing threats to the population status of individual species. We did a first exploration into the impact of fishing on Dutch Caribbean shark species following the hierarchical Ecological Risk Assessment for the Effects of Fishing (ERAEF) approach. We show the preliminary results of 14 species that were assessed using a PSA analysis and identify further data needs to effectively base future conservation action and management decisions.
9050: Studies focusing on environmental factors that influence the distribution of juvenile sharks in shark nurseries and essential habitats are still scarce in the literature. Anthropogenic stresses such as overfishing and habitat destruction urge for improved holistic conservation and fishery management approaches to respond to decreasing shark abundances in many areas. Investigating species-specific environmental preferences and identifying potential nursery areas provides much needed scientific baseline data that can support long-term decisions and aid the protection of threatened species in respective regions. In Fiji, knowledge on sharks is still limited, though scientific investigations are increasing. This study assessed juvenile shark abundances in a tropical estuary in north-western Viti Levu, Fiji, by conducting a fishery-independent survey over the course of five months. Additionally, potential abiotic drivers of juvenile shark distribution were investigated and average shark catch composition on the local fish market was monitored over a period of 67 days. Three shark species were observed within the estuary; Carcharhinus limbatus, Sphyrna lewini and Sphyrna mokarran. Depth, turbidity and proximity to mangroves were identified as the most influential drivers, although relative importance differed among shark species. The condition of umbilical scars (70 % open or semi-healed) and observed mean sizes of captured individuals strongly suggest that the Ba estuary area serves as a parturition ground for at least two of the present species (S. lewini, C. limbatus) and may consequently be utilized as a nursery ground. Thus, this study offers valuable insights into the early life-stages of three shark species in the Central Pacific.
9051: Our poor understanding of deep-water shark life history and their ecological role within continental slope environments is of concern in light of current heavy fishing pressures. The life-long movements of individual sharks govern population connectivity, potential roles in ecosystem structuring and vulnerability to fishing pressure. Unravelling individual movement behaviour is challenging in most oceanic elasmobranchs, but especially so for deep-water fishes where smart tags and mark-recapture studies are seldom practical. Here we use bulk carbon and nitrogen stable isotope analysis, of both sharks and the wider fish community, and a long-term catch-abundance survey to uncover both spatial and trophic dynamics within a bathyal shark assemblage at Rockall Trough. Furthermore, we present stable isotope data from incrementally-grown tissues from two historically exploited deep-water sharks species, the Leafscale Gulper Shark Centrophorus squamosus and the Portuguese Dogfish Centroscymnus coelolepis from the Northeast Atlantic. We report the first direct evidence for ontogenetic shifts in depth and large-scale latitudinal migrations for individual deep-water sharks within the northeast Atlantic. Isotopic evidence for individual movements compliments genetic data quantifying population-scale connectivity. Comparisons of life history movements of these species with other deep-water fishes from Northeast Atlantic allow us to explore the ecological role that these sharks play and the potential consequences of their declines. Although zero total allowable catches (TACs) are enforce within Europe, evidence provided here suggests this may only offer partial protection during the ontogenetic movements of larger, highly migratory shark species.
Session 4: Deep-water shark and related species
9052: The Velvet Belly Shark is a small deep-sea shark living in the eastern Atlantic and in the Mediterranean Sea. Despite the prohibition for deep-sea shark species, they are very sensitive to overexploitation and are facing un-reported by-catches. Moreover, deep-sea sharks have an important role in maintaining a balance in their respective food webs, and are particularly vulnerable to commercial fishing pressures due to their slow growth rates and low reproductive capacity. This is worsened by the fact that basic biological information in order to support sustainable management of fisheries at appropriate spatial scales, is lacking for this species. This paper is the result of the sampling analysis in 3 different areas of the Atlantic (n=798): the southern region of the Bay of Biscay, the Celtic Sea and the off the northeast of Scotland from 2013 to 2015 and at depths between 400 and 500 meters. This study measured the maturity stage range between local distributions to assess ecological parameters in a deep-sea shark, Etmopterus spinax, and discusses impacts on their conservation.
Session 4: Deep-water shark and related species
9053: Classic shark taxonomy has been historically based on biometric relationships between body measurements. Nevertheless, variations during ontogeny or due to sexual dimorphism often have not been taken into account. This situation makes difficult the correct identification and new descriptions of species of the genus, which is essential for conservation and fisheries management issues. Morphometric trends of 73 body measurements in the mesopelagic shark Etmopterus spinax from 116 specimens caught in the Gulf of Valencia (Western Mediterranean) have been studied. Existence of sexual dimorphism has been detected in only 9.5% of such measurements, but 97.3% showed allometric trends at least in one of the sexes. A remarkable allometric trend revealing the existence of appreciable differences of shape between new-borns and adults has been detected in 27% of measurements. Among these, it is remarkable a clear negative allometric trend in cephalic and caudal regions, a positive allometry in visceral region and different trends, but close to isometry, of most measurements related with paired fins. Ontogenetic variation of several taxonomic characters used in taxonomy of the genus Etmopterus has been analysed. Such characters, defined as ratios between body measurements, have shown a high variability due to morphometric changes during ontogeny. The presented results intend to provide a pattern of ontogenetic changes that could be extrapolated to related species, to stablish useful taxonomic characters for the genus. In this sense, we suggest the use of body measurements characters showing in E. spinax isometric patterns, or with ratios among measurements showing similar allometric coefficients.

9054: Although, 50 shark species are described as luminous, their ecology is still poorly known while they represent about 10 percent of all shark species. One small deep-sea model shark species, Etmopterus spinax (Linnaeus 1758), living in eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean Sea, has attracted a lot of attention. Studies have shown that E. spinax use the luminescence to avoid predators by a camouflage called counterillumination (when emitted light is similar than downwelling sunlight at depth, to cloak the silhouette from below). Other studies have shown that the regulation of its light intensity is hormonal and therefore is very slow. This leads to the conclusion that E.spinax, although able to counterilluminate, needed to vertically migrate in the water column in order to stay in a constant ambient light level to keep the efficiency of this camouflage. This hypothesis was called the isolume-follower. Recent work, bring some support to this hypothesis. Indeed, the swimming speed of height deep-water shark species were evaluated from footages analysis and showed that Etmopteridae luminescent sharks have a higher cruise swimming speed than non-luminescent counterparts. Here, we investigated E. spinax muscle activities through three different enzymes which can infer about the swimming capabilities of this species. Results show higher aerobic enzyme activities for E. spinax than for a non-luminescent counterpart, Centroscylium fabricii in red and white muscles. About the anaerobic enzyme activities, no significant difference is observed between both species. These results support the use of high cruise speed of luminescent sharks to fulfill the isolume-follower hypothesis.

9055: The Bluntnose Sixgill Shark Hexanchus griseus (Bonaterre, 1788) is a relatively common wide-spread deepwater shark that occurs along the outer continental shelf and upper slope. However, very little information exists about their distribution patterns, migrations and behaviour. This paper summarizes all the information collected in north of Spain waters (Galicia and Cantabrian Sea, NE Atlantic) from different surveys carried out in this area. Most of the specimens were caught in Galician waters and nearly all of them were juveniles (less than 2 years old). A priori, no relationship is observed between size and depth of capture. Data obtained from and electronic pop-up tag (Mini PAT) fixed during 75 days on one shark, provided information about depth and temperature preferences. Mean depth was 913 m ± 76.3 (depth range 727.5 -1247.0 m) and mean temperature was 10.3 ºC ± 0.2 (range 8.0-10.8 ºC). Vertical movements were done smoothly and data analysis do not show diel vertical migration or clear pattern.
Session 4: Deep-water shark and related species
9056: This study represents the first systematic data on the seasonal distribution, habitat use and genetic structure of Sevengill Shark populations in Aotearoa, New Zealand. Sharks were attracted to coastal sampling sites in Ōtākou (Otago Harbour) and Te Whaka ā Te Wera (Paterson Inlet) using chum, during 71 sampling trips conducted from July 2013 to May 2015. Sharks were implanted with stainless steel dart tags (n = 55) and photographs of unique dorsal markings (n = 23 unique individuals) were obtained. In Ōtākou, a clear seasonal pattern of Sevengill Shark sightings emerged. Sharks were detected on 85% of survey trips in summer, whilst no sharks were detected in winter or spring. In Te Whaka ā Te Wera, sharks were sighted throughout all seasons, but a decline in shark encounters occurred during winter. Both male and female Sevengill Sharks were encountered, and individuals ranged between 1.5 m and 2 m total length.
Session 4: Deep-water shark and related species
9057: Top-down versus bottom-up control of marine ecosystems has been debated for decades. Large sharks are frequently described as "apex predators" that maintain ecosystem health by controlling prey populations, but evidence to support shark-mediated top-down effects is limited. Declines in shark populations led to a surge in research seeking cascading effects of predator removals on lower trophic levels. In the northwest Atlantic Ocean, a highly cited paper in Science Magazine claimed depletion of large sharks caused dramatic increases in Cownose Ray populations which led to collapses of commercial bivalve stocks due to ray predation. These claims were used to justify a Cownose Ray fishery under the slogan 'Save the Bay, Eat a Ray'. Human consumption of the rays and killing them for sport were touted as environmentally responsible mechanisms to promote recovery of estuaries and shellfish stocks. We evaluated the evidence for this trophic cascade and found the conclusions were unsupported at all trophic levels. We demonstrated that Cownose Rays have among the most vulnerable elasmobranch life histories suggesting that current harvest rates may be unsustainable. This study highlights the danger of confirmation bias in conservation biology. Sensational scientific claims garner media attention and high citation rates by scientists, even if the studies are challenged in the literature as being severely flawed. Objectivity, scepticism and acknowledgment of uncertainty are critical components to scientific research and robust peer-review. Confirmation bias not only damages scientific credibility, but may also promote misguided conservation measures that may have negative unintended consequences.

9058: The Angelshark Squatina squatina is one of the most endangered fish species in Europe, listed as Critically Endangered. Once common throughout the Atlantic and Europe's seas, they are now extinct from much of their former range, leaving the Canary Islands as the last remaining stronghold. Whereas the presence of Angelsharks around the Canary Islands is known, information about nursery grounds and the ecology of neonates and juveniles is majorly lacking. This study investigated a unique nursery ground at Tenerife Island, using a tag-recapture study since 2015, to (1) describe habitat use and population structure, to (2) work out growth rates and (3) relativeness among juvenile Angelsharks. Surveys were only conducted at night, in sandy lower shore areas between 0.4-5 m depth. Preliminary results show that juvenile Angelsharks exhibit a long-term residency of at least 5 – 6 months. Out of 179 tagged sharks, ranging from 23-48 cm (total length), 23 were recaptured representing a recapture rate of 12.8 %. The sex-ratio approached a 1:1 ratio (89 males, 90 females). Recaptured sharks showed an estimated growth rate of 0.161 year-1. Gravid females were observed, indicating that this area might also be used as a parturition site. These findings confirm this beach as an important nursery and breeding habitat for Angelsharks and emphasize the urgent need for protection and management of this area.

9059: Environmental DNA (eDNA) is a relatively new tool for the detection of rare, threatened and invasive species in water bodies. In this study we investigated the utility of an eDNA approach in detecting the Critically Endangered Largetooth Sawfish Pristis pristis in freshwater habitats in northern Australia. Water samples were collected from a large aquaria mesocosm containing sawfish and other aquatic species, and floodplain waterholes and the main river channel of the Daly River, Northern Territory. Water samples were filtered using a 20 µm nylon filter. DNA was extracted from filters and analysed with PCR using species-specific mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase subunit 1 (COI) primers designed to amplify only Largetooth Sawfish DNA. PCR products were cleaned and the COI gene sequenced to confirm the species identity. Testing using this method using three aquaria, one containing a Largetooth Sawfish, positively identified sawfish only in the correct aquarium. In the field water samples, seven of eight floodplain waterholes produced a sawfish eDNA PCR product, while eDNA was not detected in the main river channel. Based on gillnet sampling and traditional ecological knowledge, sawfish were known to occur at half of the waterhole and floodplain sites that tested positive for sawfish eDNA. These results demonstrated that an eDNA approach to detecting Largeooth Sawfish can produce reliable results and can be used as a survey tool to help with conservation efforts for this and other threatened elasmobranchs.
Session 5: Elasmobranchs under threat: Sawfish, angel sharks and guitarfish
9060: Sawfishes (Pristidae) are facing on of the most critical conservation issue worldwide despite the increase of their protection and research. In Western Africa, the two species (Pristis pristis and P. pectinata) are still present in localised areas that deserve more investigation. Biological and ecological knowledge of rare species is a thorny challenge that may be solve by indirect methods such as tagging or genetic. A recent development of environmental DNA (eDNA) offers a smart way to post-track animal presence. By combining data from current distribution of sawfish and an experimental sampling designed for remote areas, we've been testing 4 samples from substrate and water column collected in coastal seawaters of Guinea Bissau (AMP Urok, Bijagos Islands). These results are compared and discussed with aquarium sampling in order to validate and improve this new promising field method that might be a perfect tool for conservation of sawfishes.
Session 5: Elasmobranchs under threat: Sawfish, angel sharks and guitarfish
9061: Despite their extremely fragile state in the wild, sawfish specimens are ten a penny in museum collections. Sadly, the impressive nature of sawfish rostra historically led to them being collected in large numbers and transported around the world as curiosities. Could these vast collections be used as a resource for conservation biology, or are they just lifeless ambassadors for the species they represent? A number of studies have utilised museum specimens for scientific research. Specimens that have associated locality data have been used to identify and evaluate historical ranges. Given the extent to which populations have shrunk, many specimens record the presence of sawfish in areas where they are now locally extinct. Other studies have used rostral tooth counts of sawfish specimens held in museum collections to examine sexual dimorphism, bilateral asymmetry and to elucidate morphological characters for phylogenetic studies. These example studies demonstrate that these specimens have a valid use in scientific research in a bid to protect the species in the modern day. This talk outlines the many ways in which museum collections can aid conservation biology, and how museums can make their collections available for study.
Session 5: Elasmobranchs under threat: Sawfish, angel sharks and guitarfish
9062: Sawfish family (Pristidae) is recognized as one of the most in peril elasmobranch in the world. All species of sawfishes are listed as "Critically Endangered" on the Red List from the IUCN and some populations considered as locally extinct. Due to their long rostrum, sawfishes are particularly vulnerable to fisheries and the high value of their appendice is an incentive to the black market development. Sawfishes have been subject to exploitation since the 30's in different part of the world and their populations have drastically decreased. Their most important actual threat is by-catches and their post-uses. Since, 2012, DRDH has identified more than 300 rostrums in sell on French websites. Even if this trade is considered as illegal in the Washington Convention (Annex 1), the black market remains important and it could be an incentive on sawfishes over exploitation and may accelerate their extinction. To evaluate this incentive and to find solutions, DRDH has launched MEsR-SCIE Project in 2012. The on-going program will be discussed and tools used in order to prevent this illegal market and to sensitize sellers will be detailed: Websites monitoring, Public and Professional awareness, collaboration and exchanges with French Customs and moreover, legal action against professional taken by DRDH and France Nature Environnement (FNE).
Session 5: Elasmobranchs under threat: Sawfish, angel sharks and guitarfish
9063: ANGELSHARK-ID is a project created for long-term monitoring of Angelsharks Squatina squatina in the Canary Islands, employing photo-identification as a tool to generate scientific base knowledge contributing to the development of effective species management, while minimizing research impacts to the studied populations. This initiative responds to the need of obtaining evidence-based solid data sets that can help in the assessment of the populations S. squatina in the Canarian Archipelago. Observations in the wild based on non‐invasive techniques such as photo-identification are a tool to produce such data. The use of body marks registered by experienced researchers during 10 years is evaluated for use in individual identification of specimen and to get insights in the population structure and minimum population size. Throughout the years, this study received support from Loro Parque Fundación, Shark Foundation and ElasmoCan. During the 2016 sampling campaigns, more than 90% of the spotted individuals were characterised and resightments included an individual that was first observed in 2007. These and other indicators suggest the viability of the innovative use of this technique as a conservation tool for S. squatina. In addition, valuable information was acquired about the activities that Angelsharks develop in the Canarian Archipelago for their survival, a tissue data bank was established for genetic assessment, and possible natural threats were recognized.

9064: The protection of the Angelshark Squatina squatina in its last remaining stronghold is of upmost importance. This unique species has been eliminated throughout much of its historical range over the past century and is listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (Ferretti et al. 2015). However, the Angelshark is still frequently encountered in the Canary Island archipelago, giving hope that this species can be saved from extinction. In June 2016, a workshop was organised by the Angel Shark Project, IUCN Shark Specialist Group and The Shark Trust to bring a multi-disciplinary group of divers, scientists, conservation organisations, local and international shark experts alongside the Canary Island Government and Spanish Government to develop the Angelshark Action Plan for the Canary Islands. The highest priority threats to Angelshark populations were identified and key steps to address these threats were discussed to build a comprehensive Action Plan. Our joint Vision for the Action Plan is that Angelsharks in the Canary Islands are abundant and protected in their unique stronghold. The Action Plan will be launched in Autumn 2016 and focuses around six main goals: Fisheries, Habitat & Pollution, Human Interaction, Legislation, Research and Community Engagement. All interested parties are invited to participate in the Actions and become part of the newly formed Angel Shark Conservation Network. We would like to thank all the workshop participants for their detailed discussion, enthusiasm and expertise in developing the Action Plan.

9065: When working with a Critically Endangered species, in this case the Angelshark Squatina squatina, it is vital to have the cooperation of all actors involved, especially the recreational fishing community. The Angel Shark Project, have always wanted to forge a bond with everyone connected with the sea, especially the fishing and diving industries. The recreational fishing industry in the Canary Islands is extensive, with more than 130,000 licenses. In 2010, 47% of the total fishing catch was by recreational fishers. Recreational fishing in the Canary Islands can be classified into two areas: recreational fishermen and recreational fishing charter vessels where paying clients charter a boat to fish. However, there is a significant lack of data on recreational fishing activity, number of fishermen, method or species targeted. We know that at different times of year, recreational fishers use a deep or bottom method and during this period the number of Angelsharks caught greatly increase. In 2015, the Angel Shark Project developed a best practice guide to catch and release to minimize the impact and increase the survival of the Angelshark after accidental catch by recreational fishers in the Canary Island waters. In only two years we have involved more than 60% of all recreational fishing charter vessels in the Archipelago with more than 90% stake in each of the three visited islands. The success of this project lies with the continuous feedback between the Angel Shark Project, recreational fishermen and their clients with the use of community visits, questionnaires and e-messages.

9066: Sawfishes and guitarfishes share numerous characteristics: they are large, economically valuable shark-like rays found in shallow warm water close to humans that are vulnerable to capture. Scientists and managers largely failed to recognise, document, and prevent catastrophic global declines of sawfishes, making most attempts at their recovery impossible or extraordinarily difficult. However, this experience can provide valuable lessons to try and ensure the same mistakes are not made for guitarfishes: a group that remains poorly researched, with alarming declines reported for some species. Guitarfish may be even more vulnerable to extinction than sawfishes, because some species have a very restricted distribution in only the poorest developing countries. This talk outlines what elasmobranch conservation can learn both from successes and failures in the conservation of other marine vertebrates, and from the much more mature field of terrestrial conservation.

9067: Pelagic sharks are an important bycatch in pelagic swordfish longline fisheries. In the Cabo Verde Archipelago (tropical NE Atlantic), pelagic shark catches can reach important levels, sometimes higher than the target species. Due to the increased concern on the status of shark species, an EU funded project (MARE/2012/21 - SC7) was developed to provide scientific advice on the conservation of pelagic sharks associated with the EU fishing activity, in a collaboration between several EU and Cabo Verde research Institutes. A satellite tagging program was established with the deployment of 30 satellite tags in Blue and Shortfin Mako Sharks in the Cabo Verde EEZ, showing that those species are highly mobile. Stock status indicators for the main species were created, including analysis of size frequency distributions over time and standardized catch-per-unit-of-effort (CPUE) indexes. The standardized CPUEs have been stable for the past 10 years, indicating no signs of local depletion. In terms of sizes, the Blue Shark catch is composed mainly of adults, which is a sign of a healthier population. By the contrary, the catch of Shortfin Mako is composed mainly of juveniles, which is a cause of concern. The biomass and size distributions were modelled with spatial and seasonal models (GAMs) identifying locations where juveniles are predominantly concentrated and that should be prioritized for conservation. This work presents new information on the status of pelagic sharks in the Cabo Verde region, and can now be used to promote more sustainable fisheries in the region.

9068: Tope Galeorhinus galeus is a common elasmobranch throughout the NE Atlantic where landings have declined significantly with severe reductions especially notable in the Mediterranean. Previous studies have struggled to find consistent movement patterns in the region and the population is currently managed as a single stock throughout the NE Atlantic. A multidisciplinary approach consisting of tagging, both mark and recapture and archival, and genetic markers was undertaken to gain insight into Tope's regional movements and behaviour. Most Tope remained <500 km from their tagging site with some mature females displaying a wider, more southerly range including connectivity with the Mediterranean. Evidence of annual site fidelity was found in all age and sex classes. Data showed a mature male and female moving off the continental shelf to depths >800 m with some evidence of a sex dependent north/south preference. An 858-bp fragment of the mitochondrial control region (mtDNA) and eight focal microsatellite markers (µSAT) were used to explore gene flow throughout the NE Atlantic and the MED. Overall, genetic diversity was found to be relatively low with haplotype and nucleotide diversities of 0.59 and 0.001 respectively and a mean allelic richness of 4.34 in the nuclear DNA. Genetic differentiation was homogenous across sampling sites for both markers with no significant differentiation detected indicating gene flow through the NE Atlantic and Mediterranean. This work provides new insight into the movements of Tope and should be constructive to future management of the species.
9069: Identifying conservation priorities to counteract biodiversity loss has received considerable attention in terrestrial and – to lesser degree - in coral reef ecosystems. However, marine prioritisation in general remains challenged by a lack of information beyond classic geographic range maps and fishery data. Range maps and fishery data may not adequately reveal critical habitats required to sustain populations of threatened predators, which are unevenly distributed across shallow reefs, continental shelves, seamounts, and abyssal plains. Here we overcome this constraint with an extensive and novel survey to model top predator hotspots across territorial waters in the tropical Indo-Pacific using three metrics: vertebrate species richness, mean maximum body size, and shark abundance, thereby identifying critical habitats for designation of marine protected areas (MPAs). The last refuges for sharks were present at 1,200 km from markets, whereas the last refuges for body size were found at 950 km, suggesting that marine ecosystems have limited capacity to buffer shark depletions. Proximity to populations and markets combined explained 21 and 12.5 % of the variance in body size and shark abundance respectively, reflecting a human footprint that is likely to increase with developments in fishing gear and fuel efficiency. Our analyses reveals that the last predator hotspots will be supported on shallow seabed features such as seamounts, submerged banks, and continental slopes that are remote from human populations and markets. We show that these hotspots locations are currently underrepresented within MPAs deemed effective at protecting predators, and should therefore be prioritised for effective MPA designation.

9070: In April 2015 the Cayman Islands Government enacted legislation giving full protection to all elasmobranchs throughout Cayman waters. This achievement was the result of an eight year research and public awareness programme. The occurrence and abundance of sharks and rays was investigated using a) a public (diver) reporting scheme, b) extensive surveys with baited remote underwater video stations (BRUVS), and c) scientific long-lining and tagging. The data revealed moderately good populations of Caribbean Reef, Nurse and Black-tip Sharks, and smaller numbers of other species including Great Hammerhead and Tiger Sharks. Some sharks were fitted with acoustic tags, showing that Caribbean Reef Sharks may move between separate islands (up to 100 km), while the Tiger Sharks visit Cayman seasonally during migration throughout the Caribbean. Socio-economic studies demonstrated that not only is the well-known Stingray City / Sand Cay site the highest grossing tourist attraction in the Caribbean, but the possibility of seeing sharks and other marine megafauna is worth a further $100 million per year to the Caymans' economy. Public awareness projects have included talks to schools, publicity through the local brewery and a supermarket chain, outreach to fishers (including individual interviews and the formation of fisher support groups), public awareness events directed at government and other key stakeholders, and a public awareness campaign using newspapers, radio and TV. While a small minority of fishers still resent the new legislation, the overwhelming majority of both residents and visitors are highly supportive of the shark and ray protection measures.

9071: The White Shark ecotourism at Guadalupe Island is the main activity for the exploitation of this resource in Mexico. However, the use of baits has caused some concern because its effect on White Sharks at the island is unknown. Our study aims to determine the effect of different types of bait on the presence and behaviour of white sharks. The type of bait, sightings, behaviour and pictures for Photo ID were recorded aboard tourist boats that used both legal and illegal baits during August-November 2012-2014. The data were analysed according to sex, maturity and the total of sharks, in relation to the type of bait. The recording of behaviour will determine the degree of individual conditioning of white sharks, based on interaction times and consumption of baits. We recorded 6,480 sightings during 98 days, which 26% were female and 71% male (1:3 H:M; U= 1521.5; p < 0.05); 48% were identified as juveniles and 49%, as adults; for both the 3% were indeterminate organisms. Regarding to the presence according to the type of bait (n = 4), no category showed a significantly higher frequency of sightings. To describe the behaviour is necessary to conclude with the identification of individuals, but so far, has been revised 80% of the audio-visual record (n = 17,360 files). With this we have already identified 79 sharks, 21 which are new records for the population TB in Guadalupe Island.
9072: White Sharks Carcharodon carcharias are known to aggregate in areas associated with prey, such as waters around seal colonies. White Sharks at such a site, near Gansbaai, South Africa, were initially tagged with ultrasonic, active acoustic tags and manually tracked into and around areas dense in kelp and reef. Further predation studies revealed Cape Fur Seals utilise the same areas as a refuge, although the nature of sub-surface interactions between White Sharks, their prey, and ecosystem engineers remained unknown. Recent advances in biotelemetry have the potential to reveal complex behaviours within these sites. We are now deploying biologging tags with cameras, triaxial accelerometers, magnetometers, gyroscopes and depth, temperature, light and speed sensors to White Sharks in these regions. Data from these tags are providing new insights into foraging behaviours and interactions between White Sharks and their prey.
9073: We present a fully automated photo identification system for recognising the fins of individual White Sharks. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first fully automated contour-based animal biometrics system. In order to recognise individuals, we combine robust fin contour detection with a multi-scale and combinatorial representation of fin shape. This enables individual sharks to be recognised efficiently and accurately, even when images are unclear or the view of the fin is partly blocked. Overall, the photo identification system demonstrates promising performance in recognising individuals with no need for manual labelling and with an average compute time of one minute per image. On a test-bed dataset representing 85 individuals, up to 82 per cent of images are correctly classified, with a further 10 per cent of correct matches occurring within the top 10 identities returned. The objective for the current phase of the project is to integrate photo identification and online data management technologies to build a scalable and easy-to-use, multi-user white shark fin-printing database. We report the progress that has been made on this transition from our test-bed system and outline the challenges that lie ahead.
9074: Effective monitoring of pelagic shark populations in the absence of fisheries data, such as in marine reserves, is a significant challenge. Remote camera-traps have the potential to monitor pelagic sharks, but remain largely untested. Within a simulated environment, we developed a method that modified existing gas models to investigate the number of camera-traps needed to detect pelagic shark populations trends over a five-year period in both un-baited and baited (divided into full- and partial-detection) arrays. We assessed the accuracy and precision of trend estimates obtained from camera trap arrays under different scenarios of population sizes of different spatial and temporal distributions undergoing varying levels of population change. Our results demonstrated that across un-baited and both baited models, scenarios with larger starting populations, faster rates of change, heterogeneous distributions, and absence of seasonal variation required smaller camera-trap arrays to produce accurate and precise population trend estimates. We concluded that camera-trap arrays could serve as a useful fisheries-independent method to monitor pelagic sharks. However, unless the population size is large and/or changing at a high rate, significant numbers of baited camera-traps would be required. Unfortunately, such large arrays would come with significant financial and labour costs and therefore may not be a realistic monitoring option.
9075: In the Mid-Atlantic Azores, the emergence of a seasonal ecotourism shark diving industry strongly contrasts with a North Atlantic shark fishery for regional, national and foreign fleets. Shark diving may provide an economic alternative to fishing, promoting an ecological and economical sustainable use of these animals, favouring their conservation. Understanding socio-economic aspects of this new Mid-Atlantic industry is the first step towards its sustainability and ultimately shark conservation. Data were collected by means of questionnaire designed to solicit information on shark divers' knowledge, socio-economic status, expenditures and expectations, conducted between July and August 2014 on Pico and Faial Islands, to 144 divers. The majority of respondents were male (71%), between 25 and 40 years (41%), mainly from Germany, Holland and Austria, and 44% visited the Azores purposely to dive with sharks. Their response concerning overall quality of diving and diving operators was high. On average, 2.6 sharks were seen per dive and 97% of respondents did not perceive any form of shark aggression or threat. The estimated generated income of shark diving in 2014 for the Azores amounts to 1,983.347 € (around US$2,244.890). Such an amount may easily increase following the current fast expansion of (eco)tourism in the Azores and since shark diving is still on its infancy. Finally, it is worth saying that nearly 70% of participants were willing to pay an extra amount until 60€ to ensure that shark diving remains an option and more than half (53%) would like to see that amount invested in conservation.

9076: Records of rare chondrichthyan fishes to the North Sea, the transitional waters and the Baltic Sea have been collated from literature, museum collections, scientific surveys and landings data. Lusitanian species, that have their main distribution areas in more southerly and warmer waters, have likely taken migration routes during the summer through the English Channel or around the British Isles to enter the North Sea and migrated further on. Among these are specimens of Alopias vulpinus, Carcharhinus longimanus, Cetorhinus maximus, Dasyatis pastinaca, Myliobatis aquila, Prionace glauca, Pristis pectinata, P. pristis, Squatina squatina, Torpedo marmorata, and T. nobiliana, which have been recorded in the past. Boreal and deep-water species from the northern North and the Norwegian Sea, such as Chimaera monstrosa, Hexanchus griseus, Leucoraja fullonica, Rajella lintea, and Somniosus microcephalus, have done migrations probably in the winter into the area and are also presented with exceptional southerly occurrences in the southern North Sea, the Skagerrak, and Kattegat. Often, records are historic ones, showing that widely migrating specimens were able to reach the area in former times. Fisheries landings data show a rise of landings of some species in adjacent waters, such as in the Bay of Biscay or the English Channel, with a simultaneous disappearance of records of these summer guests in the considered area, indicating that fishing pressure could be responsible for their today's absence.
9077: Fisheries and aquaculture support the livelihoods of at least 10 percent of the world's population, yet 75 percent of fish stocks are either fully or overexploited, with severe declines reported for many elasmobranch species. Reversing this trend requires improved management, which depends on accurate stock status data. Yet, the majority of fisheries, in particular small-scale fisheries in the developing world, are unmonitored. Recent advances in technology and the rapid extension of mobile networks in Africa have seen new data collection systems being utilised. This study reports lessons learned from the first trial (2013-2015) using smartphones as data collection tools, in the data deficient, traditional elasmobranch fishery of SW Madagascar. A network of 13 community data collectors, along 40 km of remote coastline, were trained to record shark landings using smartphones. At the end of the trial period, data were being successfully collected by community members and sent directly to an online database, where they can be accessed instantly, facilitating quick analysis and data-sharing, providing the community, and other stakeholders with an almost real-time view of local resource use. The main challenges encountered were the lack of infrastructure, poor levels of education and limited prior knowledge of technology within the community. The project worked closely with community members to develop suitable mobile data collection and training tools. The project demonstrates that mobile technology can empower fishers and other stakeholders to collect important data to support adaptive fisheries management, and the potential for this approach to be adapted to broader-scale multi-species fisheries.
9078: Animal personality is defined as consistent individual behaviour over time and across situations, and inter-individual differences suggest different personality types. Surprisingly, in large marine vertebrates the widespread application of acoustic telemetry has rarely explored this framework to explain intraspecific variations in movement. Here, we tested if personality scores, derived from open-field tests, can be used as a proxy to predict space use in wild juvenile Lemon Sharks Negaprion brevirostris. Across two years, 29 individuals (pre-caudal length = 52.5 ± 1.7 cm) were captured in Bimini, Bahamas, and repeatedly tested in a novel open-field. Upon release they were subsequently tracked for 9 months with internal acoustic transmitters using active and passive methods. Results reveal a significant relationship between wild home-range size (kernel utilization distribution 50% and 95%) and personality in an open-field (Repeatability=0.51). Additionally, mean observed distance from shore was correlated to the personality score obtained in captivity. These results emphasize the importance of multidisciplinary approaches to movement ecology and behaviour research in large marine predators.
9079: Dogfish sharks, or Squaliformes, are a monophyletic group of sharks, which predominantly occur in the deep sea. Most former studies, either based on morphological or molecular data, support the monophyly of Squaliformes, but also result in conflicting outcomes concerning squaliform interrelationships and origination age due to different node age estimations. Herein, we use fossil tip-dating, or total-evidence to simultaneously infer phylogenetic relationships and divergence times of squaliform sharks. The dataset comprises morphological data, i.e. dental characters, and nuclear exon sequences allowing the direct incorporation of fossil and extant taxa into the divergence time estimations. The Bayesian inference analysis results in a fully resolved phylogenetic tree, supporting the monophyly of the order Squaliformes. Most fossil taxa are clustering in accordance with their taxonomic allocation in previous studies. Somniosidae is paraphyletic in respect to Oxynotidae. New findings regarding the genus-level interrelationships of Somniosidae plead for a revision of the family. The phylogenetic placement and intrageneric relationships of the extinct genus Protospinax remain unclear. The extinct Paraphorosoides ursulae (†) clusters with Etmopteridae questioning its assignment to the Dalatiidae. Node ages estimated via fossil tip-dating are mostly resulting in older ages compared to previous estimates based on calibrated molecular clocks. We estimated the origin of Squaliformes to have occurred approx. 152 Ma ago. The occurrence of bioluminescence is dated to the Lower Cretaceous before the onset of the Cenomanian-Turonian global anoxic event. Thus, luminescent organs may have already been evolved before a re-colonisation of the deep sea after the crisis.

9080: Based on their internal structure, elasmobranch teeth have been traditionally separated into two different dental histotypes, orthodond and osteodont. The orthodont histotype is characterised by teeth with an open pulp cavity surrounded by orthodentine and osteodentine, whereas in the osteodont histotype the pulp cavity is completely closed and teeth are formed only by osteodentine. However, this classification has recently been criticised because of its simplification (Moyer et al., 2015), existing species which teeth histology cannot be classified exactly within any of the classical described histotypes. To test and evaluate the variation of teeth histology within the Euselachii phylogeny, here we analysed teeth of several species of current elasmobranch using Synchrotron X-Ray Tomography Microscopy (SXRTM) to characterise their internal structure. The tridimensional reconstruction and the topographical analysis of the teeth have allowed us to identify the classic histotypes, but also describe other intermediate states, with teeth completely formed by orthodentine, or teeth with several dentine combinations in the cusp. These different arrangements could be explained by heterochronic processes affecting rates of the tissues within the teeth. Therefore, our results stand out the idea that the classical histotypes are a reductionist classification and don't reflect the real variation of this characters. The application of new methodologies, like microtomography with synchrotron, have demonstrated being a powerful tool for the study of the histology and the internal structures at submicrometric resolution.

9081: The dogfish (squaliform) sharks are dominant predators in many cool and deep seas. Most possess a unique dentition with teeth overlapping and locking together to form a continuous cutting blade on the jaw margin, either on both jaws or restricted to the lower jaw. This contrasts with the alternating pattern of teeth in almost all other sharks and rays. CT scanning of the developing teeth of the Spurdog Squalus acanthias and other squaliforms revealed that the first teeth in the embryo are arranged as in other sharks, realigning during growth to line up teeth from adjacent tooth rows. In species with more highly derived dentitions, the blade-like lower teeth first form in the embryo in a similar arrangement to in the adult of Squalus, wheres the small upper teeth retail their alternating pattern into adulthood. The possession of a unique cutting dentition allows squaliforms to feed on large food items (living or dead) when needed, giving them an evolutionary advantage in low nutrient or cold environments, where they have been focuses for their entire evolutionary history.

9082: Nursery areas provide protection from predators and ample food supply for juvenile individuals of a species, the adults of which spend their lives in different habitats. The Rewa river Delta on Viti Levu, Fiji, has recently been identified as nursery area for the Scalloped Hammerhead Shark Sphyrna lewini. We evaluated the diet composition and the trophic position of neonate and young of the year (YOY) individuals within this nursery area. The information on the diet of the sharks will provide insight on whether the nursery area provides abundant food for the sharks. For this, a combination of stable isotope analysis of shark tissue and DNA-barcoding of gut contents was used. The analysis of the carbon (δ13C) and nitrogen composition (δ15N) of muscle tissue revealed a shift in the composition which correlated with the age of the juveniles. The maternal isotope signal was evident within the muscle tissue of neonates and fades as the sharks mature. The results of the DNA barcoding of the stomach content complement the study by identifying the preferred prey species.

9083: Sharks and other polyphyodont vertebrates retain the crown gnathostome character of continuous successional regeneration of oral teeth. How capacity for successional regeneration is maintained in some lineages but lost from other (e.g. mammals) is currently unknown. We have shown that a compound and dynamic Sox2+ stem cell population resident in the shark dentition connects the superficial taste-competent oral epithelium at the taste/tooth-junction with the deep tooth-forming successional lamina via cells migrating through the lingual margin of the middle dental epithelium during successional regeneration of teeth. We have shown that both taste buds and teeth emerge from the odonto-gustatory band, a field of embryonic oral epithelium equivalent to the odonteogenic band of mammals, and that the Sox2+ stem niches of the taste/tooth-junction and the successional lamina are derived from the odonto-gustatory band. We provide evidence for the shark test-bite or taste-bite. We suggest that a novel collaboration between the generalized odontode gene regulatory network and the taste bud gene regulatory network specifically in the oropharynx was key to the evolutionary transformation between dermal odontodes (i.e. placoid scales) and oropharyngeal odontodes (i.e. teeth). Differential gene expression analyses preformed here with microdissected sub-regions of recently hatched shark dentition, including the taste/tooth-junction and successional lamina stem niches in addition to developing early teeth, erupting late teeth, and taste bud epithelium from the basihyal not associated with teeth offers novel insights into the molecular distinction between taste, tooth, and dual-competent epithelia via the discovery of shared and differentially expressed genes.

9084: Ontogenetic dietary shifts are widespread across the animal kingdom, and in many cases involve associated morphological changes in foraging phenotype. These changes may differ between sexes or vary between individuals, and are important factors in the ecology of species. While such factors have received much attention in terrestrial systems, they are much less well understood in marine taxa. The White Shark Carcharodon carcharias is a marine apex predator that is generally considered to undergo an ontogenetic dietary shift from piscivory to preying primarily on marine mammals, with an associated change in tooth morphology from cuspidate teeth suited to grasping piscivorous prey to broad teeth more capable of effectively handling large marine mammal prey. Here we integrate a new approach involving photographic analysis of live sharks, alongside data obtained from a large jaw collection and previously published data, to investigate the ontogenetic shift in tooth morphology in White Sharks, comparing this for males and females, and examining inter-individual variation in tooth shape. The results reveal significant differences between male and female white sharks in the relationship between tooth morphology and shark length (which approximates to age), and a previously unreported ontogenetic change in male tooth shape. Males develop broader upper first teeth and increased medial angle of their upper third teeth as they age, while females do not exhibit a clear ontogenetic change in tooth morphology. There was substantial individual variation in male sharks with implications for Pace of Life Syndrome, and potential phenotypic polymorphism in female sharks. The results suggest that sexual differences and individual variation play major roles in ontogenetic changes in tooth morphology in White Sharks, with potential implications for foraging biology.

9085: As abundant and widespread apex predators, elasmobranchs play influential roles in food-web dynamics of marine communities. This has obvious implications for fisheries management and marine conservation, yet elasmobranch diet is relatively understudied; for the majority of species little or no quantitative dietary data exist. This reflects the difficulties of traditional methods in the analysis of diet in wild elasmobranchs; direct observation of feeding and stomach contents analysis. Traditional methods are particularly unsuitable for those species most at risk and requiring conservation measures. Additional methods of dietary analysis are thus required. Here, by quantifying the 3D tooth surface textures that develop as a consequence of feeding, we show that tooth microwear varies with diet in sharks. 3D microwear texture analyses can be applied to both small samples and animals with no gut contents, offering a way to reduce the impact on wild shark populations when analysing their dietary ecology. This is especially relevant in the conservation of endangered species. Furthermore, because it accumulates over longer periods of time, analysis of microwear texture overcomes the 'snapshot bias' of stomach contents analysis. This is the first time that 3D microwear texture analyses have been successfully used to detect dietary differences within sharks, providing a potentially powerful tool for dietary analysis in living and extinct elasmobranchs.

9086: Whilst parasites are generally viewed in a negative light, it is possible to use their presence within their hosts for beneficial research. Using parasites as tags allows their infection to be analysed to provide information on much of the host species' ecology such as migration, diet, population growth, and to monitor the species for overexploitation. Whilst work is being done on using parasites as tags, comparatively little research effort is going into the parasites themselves and their interactions with the host species. During this research, the relationship between host species, age, sex, condition, and parasite prevalence within the Lesser-Spotted and Greater-Spotted Dogfish are analysed and investigated. The work was carried out over a period of five years, in Cardigan Bay, Wales; the area from which the dogfish samples were collected. It was found that there was a significant difference in the parasite loads of the two dogfish species (p<0.05), whereas for various reasons the other factors measured were not found to be of significance. This data will help to contribute to further study of parasites and their application as tags.

9088: An estimated one-quarter of the world's chondrichthyans are threatened with extinction (classified as Vulnerable, Endangered, or Critically Endangered) on the IUCN Red List for Threatened Species, 107 of which are rays and 74 are sharks. Julia Lawson, Programme Officer of the IUCN Shark Specialist Group (SSG), discusses the role that the SSG has played in generating action to conserve these species of concern. The SSG consists of 171 members in 55 countries who work to collectively secure the conservation, management and, where necessary, the recovery of the world's chondrichthyans by mobilizing technical and scientific expertise. Additionally, the SSG operates under the umbrella of the IUCN Species Survival Commission (SSC), an organization that first mobilized technical and scientific expertise to generate species action plans in the late 1980s. The combination of an engaged SSG membership and the senior expertise of the IUCN SSC has helped guide the development of three conservation strategies over the past five years: sawfishes (2012), devil and manta rays (2015), and the Angelshark (currently underway). These conservation strategies have drawn upon well-established conservation planning strategies, while also considering novel methods to explore the unique challenges that are faced by chondrichthyans. This talk will describe the process of developing these strategies and the conservation successes that have been achieved thus far.
9089: Since 1999, Parties to the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) have added 29 species of sharks and rays to the CMS Appendices, bringing obligations for strict protection (Appendix I) and/or cooperative conservation efforts (Appendix II). As of February 2016, all CMS-listed elasmobranchs are now also covered under the scope of a 2010 Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) -- the first intergovernmental agreement dedicated to global shark and ray conservation -- and an associated 2012 Conservation Plan. These actions have bolstered efforts to safeguard elasmobranchs through both awareness and action. Listings on the Appendices, in particular, have been a major factor in numerous domestic protections while also serving to highlight at-risk species for other international fora. Through the CMS Sharks MoU and associated Conservation Plan, signatories have agreed, inter alia, to facilitate a better understanding of shark populations and fisheries, set science-based catch limits in an effort to ensure sustainable fishing, prevent finning, and cooperate toward shark conservation through international bodies. Four years after adoption of the Conservation Plan, however, concrete actions to fulfill MoU goals remain insufficient. Considering that overfishing is the primary threat to elasmobranchs, and that many threatened populations are fished by multiple countries, the world's Regional Fishery Management Organizations (RFMOs) provide excellent opportunities for immediate, concrete action that can go a long way toward fulfilling CMS obligations and safeguarding at-risk species. Suggestions will be offered for specific courses of action, including ideas for elasmobranch scientists who interested in facilitating such progress.
9090: CITES Appendix II is intended to prevent international trade from depleting species to the extent that they become threatened with extinction. It regulates, but does not prohibit commercial trade. Such trade is only permitted if exporting countries can confirm that the products they are trading with other countries were legally obtained and if they have issued a "Non-detriment Finding" (NDF). Importing countries must ensure that this paperwork is in order before accepting the traded items. The presentation explains what an NDF is, and how trade regulation will work for the sharks and rays that were listed in Appendix II by the 17th Meeting of the Conference of Parties to CITES, in October 2016.
9091: Management of Mediterranean fisheries is a balancing act, incorporating the political, economic, cultural and environmental objectives of over 20 nations. Since 1952 this has been undertaken through the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM) whose broad remit includes the management and conservation of sharks. The GFCM can adopt binding recommendations for fisheries conservation and management which must then be implemented by GFCM Parties. In 2005 the GFCM banned fishing activities below depths of 1000m, reducing pressure on some deep-sea sharks; in 2010 and 2011 it endorsed recommendations to protect threshers and hammerheads caught as bycatch; the following year the GFCM prohibited the fishing and retention of the 24 species of threatened sharks and rays listed on the Barcelona Convention's Annex II of the Protocol concerning Specially Protected Areas and Biological Diversity in the Mediterranean – in doing so committing all Parties to implementing domestic prohibition. On paper these measures are promising. Yet huge challenges remain surrounding their implementation and enforcement. In 2016 the Shark Trust became an accredited Observer to the GFCM and is committed to working with NGO partners and the GFCM Secretariat to assist Parties in meeting outstanding obligations. The Trust is also working with partners on a 'European Angelshark Conservation Strategy', concentrating on the three Critically Endangered species found in the Mediterranean. Central to this strategy will be encouraging all GFCM Parties to fully implement recommendations outlined above.
9092: Elasmobranchs are amongst the most threatened group of marine species. Over-fishing, coupled with their life history characteristics has resulted in sharp decrease in population numbers worldwide. Identifying the population and species composition of elasmobranch species in areas of remaining known aggregations is crucial in creating a management plan to help conserve target species. The use of non-invasive survey techniques is becoming more popular in elasmobranch research. Baited Remote Underwater Video surveys (BRUV) and Underwater Visual Surveys (UVS) were applied to assess the biodiversity and relative abundance of elasmobranch species in Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park (TRNP). A total of 69 successful BRUV surveys were conducted between March – June 2015 across 3 habitats (Shallow Reef, Deep Fore-reef, Lagoon) and 2 Zones (North islet, South Islet) within the waters of Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park (TRNP), located in the middle of the Sulu Sea. A total of 11 species of elasmobranchs were documented during BRUV surveys. The surveys indicated the highest known CPUE for Whitetip Reef Shark (0.94) and Grey Reef Shark (1.2) in the world based on available data from Australia, Fiji and Indonesia. A total of 20 UVS surveys were conducted in TRNP between May 17th - 24th 2015 and June 11th - 20th 2016 showing incredibly high densities of reef sharks (7.26 per/ha-1). This study highlights the importance of properly managed protected areas for the conservation of elasmobranchs especially in regions of high exploitation and provides a unique opportunity to shift back the baseline for these vulnerable and endangered species.

9093: The Philippines was once a theatre of one of the largest Whale Shark fisheries in South East Asia though national protection in 1998 allowed the flourishing of several coastal aggregations, now supporting a growing tourism industry. Photo identification of the Philippines Whale Shark population was initiated in 1997 by WWF-Philippines in Donsol, Sorsogon. Since then, four additional aggregations have been studied. As of July 2016, 468 unique individuals have been identified in Donsol, 255 in Oslob, Cebu, 193 in Panaon Island, Southern Leyte, 98 in Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park, Palawan and 35 in Honday Bay, Palawan together with few other minor ephemeral aggregations. The 1000th Philippines Whale Shark was identified in May 2016 and uploaded on the online international database Wildbook for Whale Sharks. Data collection has been a combined effort from dedicated surveys by the Large Marine Vertebrates Research Institute Philippines, the WWF-Philippines, and citizen science. A network of connectivity between aggregations has been identified with the Bohol Sea as a major crossroads. Shark P-545 was the first Whale Shark to be matched internationally in South East Asia, covering the distance between Taiwan and Southern Leyte (>1600km) in 11 months. The trans-boundary movements of these giants is of increasing concern for their conservation in light of the continuous threats from target fisheries in Asia, and the recent listing as Endangered under IUCN Red List. Increasing fishery enforcement at national level and transnational cooperation and protection under international agreement like CMS Appendix I is strongly recommended.

9094: For the purpose of this study, the spatiotemporal distribution of Caribbean Reef Sharks Carcharhinus perezii and Nurse Sharks Ginglymostoma cirratum were described using acoustic telemetry and a long-term citizen science project. Detection indices ranged from 0.01 to 1.00 for C. perezii and 0.17 to 0.92 for G. cirratum. Overall results prove high intraspecific variation in spatial behaviour and detection patterns, especially for C. perezii. Diel detection patterns for this species suggests different behavioural patterns for some individuals associated with twilight hours. Detection pattern of G. cirratum corresponds with a nocturnal change in behaviour. The results of the citizen science program also showed a catch-per-unit-effort for each species suggesting high residency or site fidelity for both species. Significantly lower presence of C. perezii during the period January-April coincides with the parturition period known of this species, possibly suggesting partial migration for this species.
9095: Paucity of data is among the fundamental challenges in formulating any conservation effort. This difficulty is exacerbated when addressing elasmobranch research in the eastern Mediterranean Sea, where very few studies have been carried out, and historical data is scarce. Citizen science can be an effective alternative to otherwise complicated and expensive large-scale surveys aimed to evaluate species occurrence and distribution patterns. We made use of social media platforms to collect current sightings and records of elasmobranchs along Israeli coasts (Mediterranean and Red Sea), and to retrieve documentations dating back to 2005. To date, we collected over 500 records of elasmobranchs, which consisted of 15 species during a time-span of 12 years. Recorded include species that are critically endangered and/or rarely reported such as Gymnura altavela and Isurus oxyrinchus. Other reports revealed previously unrecorded events, such as large schools of Rhinoptera marginata close to shore, and large guitarfish (Rhinobatos sp.) exhibiting what seems to be mating behaviour. According to our records, the most common shark in the region Carcharhinus plumbeus shows clear variation in size throughout the year, as do Dasyatis sp., and Rhinobatos sp. Data collected from dozens of users provide a first start in creating a regional checklist of elasmobranchs in the Mediterranean, as well as provide glimpses into seasonal distributions. Records of rare and endangered species emphasize the potential benefits of record collection through the social media, as well as the major knowledge gaps of elasmobranch occurrence and distribution in the Eastern Mediterranean.
9096: Globally there are many campaigns for elasmobranchs conservation, both large and small. The overriding objective of all these campaigns is to reduce unwanted mortality in sharks and rays, but in most the focus lies on just one aspect of conservation. In order to create an improved situation over time a more encompassing approach is needed which includes the right legislation as a starting point, coordinated management to ensure the laws can be implemented, effective control and enforcement to dissuade illegal activities and active communication to stakeholders to leverage support for the new measures. Scientific work is the basis for this approach and has an important role to play in strengthening the conservation process by asking the right questions at the onset of a research project. Only by doing the science you need you can get the policy you want. We propose a science-based holistic approach to campaigning which encompasses all four essential elements: legislation, management, control and communication. Using two examples of a management system currently under development, one for the North Sea the other for the Dutch Caribbean, we showcase how such a process can be shaped.

9097: Remote atolls, such as those found within the Chagos Marine Reserve (CMR), can be connected by large, often predatory fishes that are capable of ranging between them. But the temporal patterns and dynamic nature of this connectivity can vary between species that seemingly utilise similar habitat. In this study, we focus on two species of reef-associated shark, Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos (Grey Reef) and Carcharhinus albimarginatus (Silvertip) and demonstrate, using network analyses, that they connect the northern atolls of the CMR in very different ways and that different mobility patterns have different implications for management and conservation. With Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated (IUU) fishing still a significant problem throughout the Indian Ocean, and historically minimal enforcement capacity to patrol and respond to the threat of IUU fishing within the CMR, we adopt novel methods that allow us to pinpoint key gateways and drivers of connectivity based on the movement ecology of these predators. Furthermore, we employ Bayesian techniques to infer the spatial and temporal shifts in vulnerability as these species periodically aggregate, all with a view to highlighting the times and places where enforcement is most needed to protect these species and the subsequent health of the reef ecosystem.

9098: In both fisheries & conservation, the term "shark" is often used to generalise all species as one. This makes determining species most at risk from overfishing difficult. In collaboration with the UK government, TRAFFIC developed a method to evaluate commercially-exploited aquatic species at risk of overexploitation. Life history characteristics of 61 species of sharks were evaluated to determine a score for intrinsic biological vulnerability for each of these species. Minimum age at maturity and size produced a useful approach to ranking the relative intrinsic vulnerability of species to harvesting. To determine the adequacy, or inadequacy, of existing management measures, a Management-Risk Assessment Method (M-Risk) was developed for the forty-two shark species identified as being at medium or high risk. A ranking system was developed against relevant management attributes in order to rate risk, which has the potential to assist the development of a range of conservation and fishery management measures. This can be used to support fisheries management bodies to meet obligations under MEAs such as CITES and CMS.
TRAFFIC the wildlife trade monitoring network
9099: This study describes the presence of White Sharks in relation to environmental factors during the cage diving season in Guadalupe Island. The presence of the shark at the surface and the collection of environmental data was recorded aboard tourist boats during august to November in the years 2012-2014. Data was analysed according to sex, maturity and total of sightings, for each month of the season and in relation to nine environmental factors: sea surface temperature, tide, moonlight, intensity, and the direction of wind and current, cloud cover and visibility. 6,480 sightings were recorded during 98 days. The monthly presence showed that juveniles are equally abundant throughout the season; males are particularly numerous in august and females since September, according to their migration. The effect of the environment on the presence of sharks was different to that reported for other aggregation sites in continental islands. A higher frequency of sightings was observed during temperatures between 20-23 ° C, low wind (<16 kn), low current (<0.6 kn), and high visibility values (> 17m). However, it was not possible to observe a significant effect on the overall presence of the White Shark according to the direction of the wind, current, tidal phase, moonlight or cloudiness. In general, females showed no significant relationship with the environmental factors on the surface, which could be related to sexual segregation or their trophic ecology in deep waters.
9100: A studbook is a managed breeding programme that tracks the genetics, births, mortalities and transfers across zoos/aquariums and recommends future goals/objectives for the species. It is also a point of contact and information on the species. SEA LIFE runs the European Association of Zoos and Aquaria (EAZA) studbook for Blacktip Reef Sharks Carcharhinus melanopterus. This was established in 2013 and the results are presented each year in an annual edition of the studbook. This is the third edition of the studbook and we continue to learn and build upon our experiences with Blacktip Reef Sharks. There are now 55 aquaria participating in this studbook which covers the period from 01/01/2015 until the 31/12/2015. The total number of animals has risen to 274 (124.150.0) compared to 230 (represented in 48 aquaria) in the previous studbook. Since 2007 fifteen aquaria have recorded birthing events. By documenting and then sharing the details of these breeding experiences we get one step closer to achieving a self-sustaining aquarium bred population. The studbook is looking for an in-situ research/conservation partner that also works with this species to be able to both compare and collaborate on research.
